FAST

TOKYO, Nov 11 : Japanese manufacturers' sentiment rose to its strongest level in more than five years in November as booming semiconductor demand underpinned broad-based optimism, while the non-manufacturers' mood hit its highest in over eight years, a Reuters monthly poll showed. The Reuters Tankan sentiment index for manufacturers rose to plus-27 in November, the highest reading since August 2021, from plus-22 in October. The poll, a leading indicator of the Bank of Japan's quarterly Tankan business survey, was conducted from October 27 to November 6 and received responses from 214 of 508 firms. The indexes are calculated by subtracting the percentage of pessimistic responses from optimistic ones, with positive figures indicating net optimism. The improvement in manufacturers' confidence was led by the electronics sector, where sentiment jumped to plus-39 in November from plus-25.

"Semiconductor demand, particularly for memory, is very strong," a manager at an electronics machinery company said. Sentiment in the precision machinery sector, which includes some chip-related equipment makers, also improved to plus-42 from plus-38. "Orders from both domestic and international remain robust," said a manager at a precision machinery company. Another respondent at a machinery firm said that product shipments for the semiconductor market have reached an "unprecedented level". Oil refinery and ceramics rose to plus-25 from plus-14, while chemicals improved to plus-33 from plus-27. The non-manufacturers' index surged to plus-35 in November from plus-23 to reach a level not seen since June 2018. Sentiment in information and communications rose to plus-29 from plus-8 thanks to strong orders. Services and others rose strongly to plus-43 in November from plus-19. One manager said that "tight labour market conditions persist among companies, keeping demand for talent at a high level." Looking three months ahead, manufacturers expect sentiment to edge up to plus-28 in February, while non-manufacturers see confidence easing to plus-29. Rising prices and higher interest rates weighed on both sectors, the survey found, with some firms struggling to pass on increased costs to customers.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK, Nov 10 : The US Securities and Exchange Commission said on Tuesday it completed distributions from a $40 million fund created from civil fines paid by Elon Musk and his electric vehicle company Tesla to resolve the regulator's first civil enforcement case against the world's richest person. In a filing in Manhattan federal court, the SEC asked a federal judge to close the Fair Fund, created after Musk settled the SEC case in 2018 charging him with securities fraud for posting on August 7, 2018, that he had "funding secured" to potentially take Tesla private. His posts on Twitter that day caused Tesla's shares and trading volume to spike, with the shares closing more than 6 per cent higher than when he began posting. They later fell after it became clear Musk had not lined up financing. Musk and Tesla each paid a $20 million civil fine, with sums designated for investor victims of the alleged fraud. Neither defendant admitted wrongdoing. Musk also agreed to let Tesla lawyers review some Twitter posts in advance, and give up his role as chairman.

The SEC said a claims administrator distributed $41.53 million, including interest and after deducting fees, to 3,350 eligible claimants. Those claimants received 51.7 per cent of their approved claims because their losses exceeded the Fair Fund's size. Another 3,046 claims were rejected. The SEC said the approximately $449,000 remaining in the Fair Fund will go to the US Treasury. "Distribution of the Fair Fund is now complete," the SEC said. The case is separate from the SEC case accusing Musk of waiting 11 days too long in March and April 2022 to disclose his early purchases of Twitter shares. Musk settled that case by having a trust in his name pay $1.5 million, also without admitting wrongdoing. A federal judge approved that settlement in July, while expressing "significant misgivings" about whether the SEC let Musk off too easily. Musk is a former adviser to Republican US President Donald Trump. He bought Twitter in 2022, renamed it X, and later folded the social media platform into his rocket and satellite company SpaceX.

WASHINGTON, Nov 10 : The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission has warned prediction market startup Kalshi of imminent charges in a probe into whether it properly notified the agency about dozens of new products, a person familiar with the matter said on Tuesday. The regulator's notification to the company suggests the charges could come soon, said the person who requested anonymity because the decision is not yet public. Kalshi in a statement said the CFTC's warning "is about a procedural error involving the submission of a handful of contracts, many of which weren't live." "We are already addressing the issue," the company added.

The CFTC did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Kalshi has rapidly expanded its product offerings since securing a legal victory over the CFTC in 2024, allowing it to list diverse event-based derivatives. However, critics of prediction-market platforms such as Kalshi and peer Polymarket argue that the products resemble gambling and could encourage addictive behavior.  In recent months, Kalshi has pursued a broader strategy of competing with traditional exchange operators such as CME Group and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange by expanding beyond event contracts into a range of asset classes through perpetual futures. Perpetual futures, often called "perps," are derivative contracts with no expiry date, allowing traders to hold positions indefinitely without rolling them over. They can also involve high leverage, increasing both potential gains and losses.  The company raised $1 billion at a $40 billion valuation late last month, co-led by Sequoia and Wellington, underscoring the growing popularity of such markets and strong institutional interest. Politico reported about the imminent charges earlier in the day.

FAST

Nov 10 : CoreWeave expects to turn profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028, executives said on Tuesday, as the AI cloud firm sought to reassure investors that strong demand and customer commitments could support its debt-fueled expansion. Shares of the Nvidia-backed company were last up about 5 per cent in volatile extended trading. The stock has crashed more than 40 per cent in the past month after CoreWeave emerged as the focal point of growing AI bubble fears, with investors worried about heavy borrowing for setting up data centers against the backdrop of rising interest rates and the pace of returns on the massive investments. The steep selloff also triggered a broader crisis of confidence in the AI trade, a sentiment amplified by the Democrats' sweeping win in the US midterms that has fueled expectations of tighter regulation in the data-center build-out.

Earlier in the day, AI juggernaut Anthropic kicked off a roadshow for its share sale at a lower target valuation than earlier estimates. CoreWeave has never turned a profit, according to data compiled by LSEG, and had about $46.9 billion in total debt as of the end of September. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator sought to ease some of those concerns on Tuesday, disclosing that the AI cloud company had $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits that are expected to flow in over the next three months. "Customer contracts come first, and investment follows. Because CoreWeave's investments are tied to committed demand, lenders have something concrete to lend against and customers typically help fund the buildout," he said in a statement. The company said it would not tap unsecured debt markets at current yields and had no need to, banking on cash flow from existing customer commitments to repay outstanding debt and additional borrowing needed to fulfill those contracts. CoreWeave's contracted revenue backlog stood at $132.5 billion at the end of September, rising from $104 billion at the end of June. At the same time, its quarterly capital spending jumped to $14.5 billion from $9.4 billion in the prior quarter. Recent earnings reports from hyperscalers also hinted at delays in data-center projects and a slower ramp in spending. Among CoreWeave's stacked roster of customers are Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic. CoreWeave now expects 2026 revenue to be between $13.0 billion and $13.3 billion, from $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion earlier. It also lifted the lower end of its annual spending target by $2 billion, now projecting spending of $37 billion to $39 billion. CoreWeave's third-quarter revenue surged nearly 170 per cent to $3.66 billion, beating estimates of $3.55 billion, while a per-share loss of 95 cents came in smaller than estimates for a $1.16 loss, according to data from LSEG.

Source: Reuters

FAST

LONDON, Nov 10 : British horse racing's welfare board on Tuesday unveiled a five-year strategy that will use AI, wearable technology and lifetime tracking of horses to prevent injuries, reduce falls and improve horses' well-being away from the racetrack. The new strategy sets out 20 priorities to improve welfare and safety of thoroughbred horses throughout their lives, spanning areas including veterinary research, injury prevention, the training environment and aftercare and extending the scope of oversight from foaling through training to life after racing. Horse racing is Britain's second most-watched sport but concern for equine welfare remains its biggest reputational challenge, with falls, fatalities and the treatment of horses at key racing festivals like Cheltenham and Aintree under constant public scrutiny. Fatality rates in jumps racing were largely unchanged at 0.47 per cent in 2025 even after measures to improve the safety of fences like changing the colour of markings in 2022.

The British Horseracing Authority says it extended the scope of its reporting to cover more horses in 2021 and that it would take time for the safety improvements to take full effect. The rate of fallers dropped below 2 per cent on a five-year average for the first time in 2025, BHA data shows.  Work to improve safety and reduce fatalities is ongoing and a priority for the sport, Minette Batters, independent chair of the Horse Welfare Board, told reporters. "It's never going to be a case of accepting fatalities," she said. "It's what can we continue to do to make the sport safer that sits front and centre of everything we're doing."  Collecting more data on all aspects of a horse's life will enable trainers, vets and racecourse officials to spot issues like weakness or heart problems before they lead to on-racecourse injuries, racing experts said. This can start as early as birth by educating breeders on how antibiotic use in foals can impact soundness or in training by using heart monitors and wearable tech to detect equine illness or underperformance. "We're standing at the beginnings of a technology revolution in training of horses, in management of horses," said Fred Barrelet, veterinary surgeon and independent member of the Horse Welfare Board. "It's also becoming accepted and part of the young next generation of trainers and breeders' repertoire and armoury for managing their horses." The strategy also includes an ambition to track the full lifetime of all horses bred for racing in Britain through the Retraining of Racehorses programme.

FAST

NEW YORK, Nov 10 : Technology shares were in the red again on Tuesday, with Anthropic's steps toward a big IPO failing to calm general anxiety about the health of the AI sector. Selling was driven by a hot US inflation report that increased expectations the Federal Reserve will raise rates again next month, alongside Nvidia's hiring lawyers for an internal investigation tied to its CEO and the development of an Ohio data center getting more complicated.  Many investors remained optimistic about the prospects for AI investments while allowing that volatility has become a fact of market life this fall. The Nasdaq Composite was off 1 per cent on Tuesday afternoon. Over the past month, the index has dropped by 1 per cent or more eight times and risen by 1 per cent or more six times.  "There is concern about what happens at the top at Nvidia, and if he's replaced, who's he replaced with," said Tim Ghriskey, senior portfolio strategist at Ingalls & Snyder in New York, who said he sees selling in Nvidia and other major AI firms as buying opportunities. "But I don’t see Nvidia falling apart. I see a very strong company hit by something not of its own making."

Besides Nvidia, down 6.5 per cent, the major decliners were mostly big beneficiaries of the AI rally that swept markets for the first two-thirds of this year. Server maker Dell Technologies was down 4.8 per cent on Tuesday but up 161 per cent for the year, according to LSEG data, while chip firm Sandisk was down 4.5 per cent for the day and up 257 per cent for the year. Among the neoclouds, smaller AI infrastructure firms that have been under pressure this month amid concerns about their capacity to raise funds under tighter market conditions, Iren dropped 10 per cent, Nebius fell 7 per cent and CoreWeave slid 3 per cent. All three have declined by at least 40 per cent since the Nasdaq hit its most recent high on October 6. CoreWeave is due to report earnings after the close on Tuesday. Many investors said they thought general market anxiety was behind much of the selling, despite a newsy day across AI-related subjects. British cloud services provider Nscale is considering delaying a $35 billion stock market listing, The Telegraph reported on Tuesday. Shares of power equipment maker GE Vernova slid more than 6 per cent on Tuesday, after Japanese investment firm SoftBank revised equipment procurement plans for its US data center projects. GE Vernova is among the companies involved in the development of SoftBank's colossal gas-fired power plant and data center in Pike County, Ohio, analysts said. Nvidia’s was on track to shed more than $470 billion in market value over two sessions as concerns mounted over the fallout from CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing.  Even so, investors were mostly focused on the longer-term picture.  "We can always ascribe a reason as to why things are more volatile. And they have been more volatile the last few weeks for sure, since October, let's call it," said Jason Ware, chief investment officer at Albion Financial Group in Salt Lake City, Utah. "But at the end of the day, the path for stocks over the coming weeks and months is going to be really a story of earnings." Following Tuesday’s inflation report, many investors will be focusing on the next big events for technology stocks, which stand to be Nvidia’s earnings report after the close a week from today and Anthropic’s IPO in the days after, regardless of what stocks do on a given day.  “We're probably gonna have record earnings again next year unless we see a recession or a massive pivoting on AI capex, and I don't expect either one,” said Ware, whose firm owns Nvidia. “And so I think that's going to be the signal is the trajectory of earnings, the economy growing more than 2 per cent. And the rest of this is sort of just short-term noise that will, like I said, get ironed out over time."

Source: Reuters

The AI giant on Tuesday filed an updated prospectus for its IPO, seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, slightly short of some investors' expectations. Anthropic's IPO is seen as a key test of Wall Street's faith in the AI boom it helped ignite.

NEW YORK, Nov 10 : US electricity consumption will rise to record highs in 2026 and 2027 due to power-hungry AI data centers and electrification, the US Energy Information Administration said in its Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) on Tuesday. The EIA projected that power demand will rise from a record 4,216 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) in 2025 to 4,306 billion kWh in 2026 and 4,370 billion kWh in 2027. If correct, 2026 would be the third year in a row of record demand. Demand is surging largely due to data centers dedicated to artificial intelligence. Homes and businesses have also been relying more on electricity and less on fossil fuels for heat and transportation. The EIA forecast that power sales in 2026 will rise to 1,546 billion kWh for residential consumers, 1,557 billion kWh for commercial customers and 1,061 billion kWh for industrial customers.

As renewable output rises, the EIA said the share of power generation from coal will slide from 17 per cent in 2025 to 15 per cent in 2026 and 2027, while the share of natural gas in 2026 will hold steady from 2025 at 40 per cent, then ease to 39 per cent in 2027. The percentage of renewable generation will rise from around 24 per cent in 2025 to 25 per cent in 2026 and 28 per cent in 2027, while nuclear power's share will hold at 18 per cent in 2026 and 2027, the same as in 2025, according to the outlook. The EIA projected that gas sales in 2026 would slide to 12.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) for residential consumers and 9.4 bcfd for commercial customers, but rise to 23.8 bcfd for industrial customers and 37.4 bcfd for power generation. Those figures compare with all-time highs of 14.3 bcfd in 1996 for residential consumers, 9.9 bcfd in 2025 for commercial customers, 23.8 bcfd in 1973 for industrial customers, and 36.8 bcfd in 2024 for power generation.

Earlier in the day, Anthropic launched a roadshow for its highly anticipated US initial public offering, with plans to raise as much as $64.4 billion at a $1.02 trillion valuation. WASHINGTON, Nov 10 : Alphabet's Google has agreed to additional privacy protections in the acquisition of employee data from defunct Spirit Airlines, a union representing employees said Tuesday. The agreement clears the way next week for approval of Google's $10 million deal to acquire Spirit data to train AI models. The union said it had won a more rigorous de-identification process than previously planned and added significant employee data will be excluded from the sale, including health and medical information. As part of Spirit's closure and asset liquidation, Google won an auction in August for data from emails, spreadsheets and calendars, as well as for marketing, productivity and operations. Spirit Airlines halted operations in May. A bankruptcy judge is now set to approve the deal next week.

A group of about 120 lawmakers raised concerns last month about the data sale. Last month, a privacy ombudsman recommended a US bankruptcy judge approve the deal after excluding passenger personal information from 97 million Spirit customers. The lawmakers, led by Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, and Representative Steven Horsford, a Nevada Democrat, said the sale would include 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams messages and other employee records. Spirit Airlines said it was pleased to have reached a resolution with labor unions as it continueed to maximize value for its creditors. "We are grateful for the collaboration of Google, the consumer privacy ombudsman, our labor unions, and other key stakeholders who are engaging with us constructively on this sale," a spokesperson said. Google, which did not immediately comment Tuesday, said last month it did not want to acquire personal information. "We are not looking to buy any personal information from Spirit. The information will either be completely excluded or will be de-identified by an independent third party before Google receives any data," Google said last month.

TAIPEI, Nov 10 : TSMC plans to invest up to $1 billion across leading AI developers Anthropic and OpenAI, highlighting the Taiwanese chipmaker's confidence in long-term demand for the technology even as concerns grow about soaring AI spending. The company is positioning itself to benefit not only from supplying AI infrastructure, but also from owning stakes in some of the industry's most influential developers. TSMC's board approved on Tuesday an investment of up to $500 million to acquire shares in Anthropic at its initial public offering price, and an investment of up to $500 million to acquire preferred stock in OpenAI. The move comes after Anthropic on Tuesday priced its initial public offering at $70 to $78 per share, seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion in what would be one of the largest stock market debuts on record.

The Claude maker is also raising $26 billion through a separate private placement backed by investors, including Alphabet's Google, Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft. TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker and a critical supplier to leading AI firms, including Nvidia, whose pricey graphics processors underpin many of today's AI models. Last month, TSMC reported a sixth consecutive quarter of record profit and said demand for AI-related chips remained "extremely robust," even as it adopted a cautious outlook for 2027. The company expects full-year 2026 revenue growth of about 44 per cent and said demand continues to outstrip its manufacturing capacity. TSMC is also expanding production, including a $265 billion investment in manufacturing facilities in Arizona and an evaluation of potential projects in Texas.

Nov 10 : Amazon's Ring on Tuesday launched a new robotics business with two autonomous security products, a flying indoor camera for homes and a roving security robot designed for businesses, as the company expands beyond its established lineup of home-security devices. • Both devices - Ring Drone and Ring Rover - use Ring's AI Pilot system, which combines cameras, vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing to map spaces, identify potential patrol points and navigate around obstacles, Amazon said • The launch marks an expansion of Ring's security business, which began with video doorbells and has grown into a broader network of connected cameras, sensors and alarms. • The company said the new robots are designed to work with the existing devices through the Ring app

BERLIN, Nov 10 : German defence firm Helsing will present new artificial intelligence-based military targeting software on Wednesday, seeking to benefit from growing concerns among European governments about relying on US companies such as Palantir. After President Donald Trump's repeated threats to quit NATO, concerns over dependence on Washington and data sovereignty have fuelled resistance against US data analytics and defence software firm Palantir in parts of Europe. The company makes the best-known military AI system of its kind, the Maven Smart System, which has been deployed by the US, NATO commands and several NATO members. In the invitation to the Berlin presentation of its system, Helsing said it was "crucial that we be able to conduct precise reconnaissance, make the right decisions in the face of uncertainty, and act with precision on the battlefield, with autonomy and without dependencies: from Europe and for Europe".

The war in Ukraine has shown the value of AI tools in dramatically speeding up battlefield decision-making by rapidly processing and interpreting vast streams of data generated by drones, satellites and other sensors. PALANTIR INSISTS CUSTOMERS ARE IN FULL CONTROL Palantir has insisted its customers are in full operational control of the software that they buy from the company and that it does not have a "kill switch" to deactivate it remotely. Concerns over dependence on the US were exacerbated last month after speed restrictions for Ukraine's Starlink terminals hampered Kyiv's efforts to intercept Russian drones and forced some operations to be cancelled. In June, the Trump administration moved to block non-US residents from Anthropic's most advanced models, Mythos and Fable, on national security grounds, prompting the AI company to abruptly suspend access to the models globally. The ban was lifted later the same month, but European lawmakers still warn the episode showed that the US holds a "kill switch" over essential technologies that it is more than willing to use. The German military has made clear that, for now at least, it will not buy Palantir's Maven for its forces. The country is aiming to deploy its own AI-powered system from 2027, with full implementation expected in 2028.

Source: Reuters
